title: Your Church May Know Less Bible Than You Think (And What to Do About It)
summary: A new survey indicates Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it.
summary_zh: 一项新的调查显示，基督徒已经屈服于该文化的普遍识字危机。“书中的人”不读它。
title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second. The sermon matters enormously. But we’re le

title: Does Christianity Make Sense? On God, Evil, and the Ache (with Gavin Ortlund)
summary: Gavin Ortlund joins Collin Hansen to discuss apologetics and why Christianity makes sense.
summary_zh: 加文·奥特伦德（ Gavin Ortlund ）与科林·汉森（ Collin Hansen ）一起讨论了护教学以及基督教为什么有意义。
title_zh: 基督教有意义吗？论上帝、邪恶和痛苦（与Gavin Ortlund合作）
content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
summary_zh: 今天，大多数基督徒将这两个福音方面视为同一个圣经馅饼的一部分。但我们往往看不到它们必然交织在一起。
title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). This gospel of the kingdom must be lived out through embodied acti
content_zh:
2016年至2018年,任社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在脸书和推特上,

如果你读过我的文章, 你可能没有猜到 我成长在一个保守的基督教家庭 在郊区, 或者我每天的教育, 从4岁开始在基督教学校。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.

然而,这个以福音为本的我青年世界被故意洗涤,并在仅仅10分钟之内就脱离了贫困和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距时,我成了在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我的成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.

自2001年起, 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教堂里有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻居之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。

所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。

我开始看到圣经福音中的两个方面。 让我们称之为十字架的福音和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救和接纳信徒作为自己的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 在罪恶中,我们是他的敌人。

在基督中,我们相信好消息,我们与上帝和解(5:6-10室),并保证与上帝永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写的那样,“基督也曾因罪恶而受苦,善人因不义者而受苦,以便他把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。

此外,福音的交叉方面强调,受委托传达这一信息的人必须与一个迷失和垂死的世界分享(Matt. 28:18-20)。 十字架的福音必须预告;必须宣布。 这是优先事项。 从这个福音中流传着每一个好礼物.

我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。 王国的福音是好消息,上帝对正义、善良与和平的意志已经释放。 作为上帝的子孙,信徒们被邀请在确保王国使命取得成果方面发挥作用。

耶稣在部里首先发出一个信息,宣称“向穷人提供好消息”和“向......受压迫的人提供自由”(公爵4:18)。 他呼吁他的听众悔改,包括他们压迫和忽视穷人的方式(Matt. 3:2;4:17)。 他特别斥责法利赛人忽视“较重要的法律事项:正义、慈悲和忠诚”(23:23)。

保罗也教导道,福音不仅使我们与上帝团聚,而且通过在教会中调和分裂的人民来伸张正义。 他写道,“[基督]自己是我们的和平,他使我们两个[种族群 都成了和平,并用他的肉体打破了敌对的分隔墙”(Eph 2:14)。

我们履行法律,通过我们作为立法者的身份,活出福音的王国影响(马特:9)。 福音的王国方面为我们提供了追求上帝的旨意的愿景,即 " 在地上像在天上一样 " (6:10),即看到一切事物都变新(Rev.21:5)。 王国的福音 必须通过神圣的 行动而存在
author: Ben Sciacca

title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
summary_zh: 在政治危机时期，我们可以从马丁·劳埃德-琼斯（ Martyn Lloyd-Jones ）的事工中学到三个教训。
title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
summary_zh: “少滚动，多活”可以帮助青少年和家长培养他们所需的技术技能，从而过上扎根于现实、充满智慧的生活。
title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. title: Effective Altruists and the Spreadsheet Gospel
summary: Effective altruism commands us to love our neighbor yet dissolves that neighbor into a statistic. It asks for the fruit of the image of God while denying the root.
summary_zh: 有效的利他主义命令我们爱我们的邻居，但却把那个邻居溶解成一个统计数字。它要求上帝形象的果实，同时否认根源。
title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. 在过去十年中,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷生根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是它的思想决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。

经济学人最近称这个哲学是“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称这个运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。

作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能兑现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音不相干,并且是一个糟糕的代名词。 什么是有效的替代主义?

2000年代后期和2010年代初,有效的利他主义从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和以证据为基础的慈善活动趋同而出.

澳大利亚学者彼得·辛格以他1972年的论文"饥荒,富裕和道德"为重要基础,他在该作中认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务. 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。

有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。

“有效替代主义中心”解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。

随着几个慈善组织的成立, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“高影响”职业。

他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球卫生、动物福利和经济差距的努力。

在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后人和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期的未来是我们时代的主要道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的,应该加以权衡,而且可能有上万亿美元。

许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来预防风险, 即使这饿死今天的好原因, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能等关注。

对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对AI可能启示录的担忧解释了为什么该运动在AI研究、AI公司以及AI的倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究人员和硅谷科技流派中有自然的读者,

title: New Free Playlist: 30 Songs of Gratitude to God
summary: Brett McCracken curates a playlist of 30 songs to help you practice gratitude to God—not just on Thanksgiving but every day.
summary_zh: 布雷特·麦克拉肯（ Brett McCracken ）策划了一个包含30首歌曲的播放列表，以帮助您不仅在感恩节，而且每天都对上帝表示感谢。
title_zh: 新的免费播放列表： 30首感谢上帝的歌曲
content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. You can access the playlist now on Spotify and Apple Music . Enjoy! title: The Voice of the Martyrs: Prayers of the Persecuted
summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.
summary_zh: 我们祈求正义，但我们是作为被饶恕的罪人祈求正义。
title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. title: Martin Luther in 5 Latin Phrases
summary: Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift.
summary_zh: 耶稣完美的生命和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。因此，神的义不仅仅是他的审判。这也是他的天赋。
title_zh: 马丁·路德的5个拉丁短语
content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. content_zh: 马丁·路德于1483年11月10日生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入了曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了艾索普的"寓言". 从早年到后来在马格德堡的寄宿学校学习,路德是一名勤奋的学生。 他跟上了拉丁语,几个重要的拉丁语短语也出现在路德的著作中. 其中5个是他的生平和首席神学重心的良好总结. 1. Iustitia Dei 1505年7月,路德被猛烈的雷暴所困. 惊慌惊恐地与上帝讨价还价,许诺成为和尚. 进入修道院后,路德再次被恐惧所克服. 当他第一次作为牧师主持弥撒时, 相反,充满了颤抖。 随着礼拜的开始,路德在礼拜堂前取而代之,他开始背诵拉丁语祈祷. 路德知道上帝在判断上是完美的,并且完全没有罪恶. 因此,当他想到了iustitia Dei“上帝的公义”(1:17)时,恐怖袭击了他。 传记家罗兰·H·班顿(Roland H. Bainton)描述了困扰路德思想的思想:我该向神圣的陛下举起手来, 众天神围绕他. 在他点头的时候,大地会颤抖... ...但是,我是灰尘和灰烬。 当路德拿起面包和葡萄酒时,他摇得这么厉害,差点把杯子掉下. 在那些年里,路德在学校和修道院里长大,他只把上帝的正义或正义视为他对人类罪恶的积极判断。 他后来写道, 虽然我作为一个和尚生活 没有责备, 我感觉和知道我是上帝面前的罪人。 我有一个极度不安的良心。 我憎恨惩罚罪人的善良之神 2. 1512年,路德成为维滕贝格的大学教授. 当他为他的演讲而学习圣经时,他开始在新的光芒下看到上帝的正义. 路德看到耶稣基督如何对待我们的人性,他如何过上完美的生活并死于十字架上的痛苦而可耻的死亡来取取罪的惩罚. 他看见了上帝如何使耶稣从死地复活,以及他现在如何通过信仰为基督徒辩护. 上帝宣布,在他看来,耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的救赎天赋。 耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡是所有信徒的计数. 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的天赋。 当路德做出这个发现时发生了什么? 他是这样描述的 : “ 我感到我再次出生,并通过开放的大门进入了天堂。 ” 在那一天之后,路德开始教导上帝给予基督徒“外星人的正义 ” , 即“来自我们以外的”一种格外不义的正义。 我们的正义不是来自我们, 祈祷, 我们的正义最终被发现 并属于另一个,我们的救主耶稣基督。 3. Crux sola est nostra Godologia 1517年10月31日,路德将他的"95个本事"出名地贴在了城堡教堂的门上. 路德在书中明确表示反对教皇利奥十世和德国自己的勃兰登堡阿尔贝特亲王赞助的集资宽恕计划。 次年,即1518年4月,路德在海德堡举行的奥古斯丁会令春季会议上为这些观点辩护. 路德在恐惧中走去开会. 他期望那里的领导人严厉斥责他。 这毕竟是教皇要求他们做的。 但令路德惊讶的是,与会领导人激动地欢迎他的辩护. 路德怎么说 他的新朋友这么兴奋? 路德在他的"海德堡争论"中描述了两类人——"荣耀之神"和"十字架之神". 这个

title: ‘Mosquito Bowl’: Football Stars on the Front Lines
summary: Peter Berg’s ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ is essentially ‘Friday Night Lights’ meets ‘Hacksaw Ridge.’
summary_zh: Peter Berg的“The Mosquito Bowl”本质上是“周五夜灯”与“Hacksaw Ridge”相遇。
title_zh: “蚊子碗” ：前线的足球明星
content: Peter Berg’s The Mosquito Bowl is essentially Friday Night Lights meets Hacksaw Ridge . It’s a movie with the same creative vibe as Friday Night Lights (gritty handheld camera, muted color palette, Explosions in the Sky post-rock soundtrack) but applied to a brutally violent true story of WWII’s Battle of Okinawa, one of the single bloodiest battles of the 20th century. Also like Berg’s Friday Night Lights , The Mosquito Bowl ( out now in theaters ; coming to Netflix November 25) is based on a book by Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist Buzz Bissinger . The 2022 book—subtitled A Game of Life and Death in World War II —only has one chapter (of 41) devoted to the actual 1944 football game dubbed “The Mosquito Bowl.” Most of the book is about the war, and the young men who left wives, kids, and promising NFL careers to fight it. Likewise, Berg’s film adaptation is mostly a somber, unflinching WWII film, with a brief reprieve of joy in the form of a football game on Guadalcanal between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division. Just as in Friday Night Lights , where the drama of high school football parallels the struggles and triumphs of life off the field, the football game in The Mosquito Bowl parallels the “game of life and death” that surrounds the men at war. Sports are interesting in this way: They provide escape from real life but also training for it, an arena of danger and high stakes but not ultimate stakes. Sports often map onto life—we draw up plans and plays but have to improvise; we get hurt but can heal; we thrive individually through teamwork; sometimes we win and sometimes we lose. Yet sports are unlike real life too. Winning or losing on the field is a matter of trophies and glory, but off the field, it can be a matter of life and death. Young Men Willing to Fight and Die The Mosquito Bowl (rated R for graphic war violence and language), opens with a well-known epigraph from Herbert Hoover : Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. The movie opens with muddy college football scenes in the fall of 1941, as the four central characters are introduced: John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Brown quarterback; Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), University of Wisconsin tackle; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Purdue fullback; and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), Wisconsin end. They were all-star athletes with promising futures. Many of them were collegiate All-Americans and drafted by NFL teams. Yet December 7, 1941, happened, and their futures were all changed. Once bound together by football skill, friendly rivalry, and fierce competition on the gridiron, these men soon bonded in a different setting: as marines in WWII’s savage Pacific theater. Instead of fighting for yards on the field, they fought for ground in a war of attrition on Okinawa. Instead of a football in hand, they carried guns and bayonets. Instead of tackling their opponents, they wrestled them to the death in hand-to-hand combat. Like many in the Greatest Generation, these men volunteered to enlist and fight. The Mosquito Bowl celebrates their duty and sacrifice. In one scene, Baumann’s younger brother says, “You don’t have to go,” to which Baumann replies, “I do. I’m needed.” It’s hard to imagine star athletes, whether collegiate or professional, volunteering to go to war in 2026. But in 1943, it was normal. Okinawa, Bissinger writes in the book, was “by far the largest collection of athletes ever to die in a single battle.” And in the entirety of WWII, 21 NFL players died in combat, as well as two players from Major League Baseball. Why were they so willing to lay down their lives? Perhaps back then, men had the bigger hori

title: Pastor, Be Opportunistic
summary: Pastor, you cannot afford to coast. You cannot afford autopilot. Be a gospel entrepreneur. Eternity is at stake.
summary_zh: 牧师，您负担不起海岸。您买不起自动驾驶仪。成为一名福音企业家。永恒岌岌可危。
title_zh: 牧师，抓住机会
content: My coffee had gone cold as the church planter mourned that his church felt stagnant. Worse than not growing—a thick malaise had settled over the congregation. The first three years were exciting; the community was intrigued by a new church plant, genuinely curious about what it was all about. But everything had plateaued. Leaders grew complacent. Sundays—even with strong preaching—felt cold and passionless. The church’s reason for existing had shrunk to feeding and caring for the Christians who already called it home. The church planter couldn’t see how it was still transforming the community. An older mentor at the table cleared his throat. “I’m sorry to hear that. Let me ask you—what is one risky, hard thing the Lord is inviting your church to do that you’re hesitant to do?” The planter scratched his head. “I don’t know. I’ve never been asked that before.” The older man shrugged. “Every pastor should be ready to answer that question. If he can’t, he needs to spend some time praying and fasting until he can. Comfort and complacency are incredibly dangerous.” I’ve sat in enough of these conversations to know that wise, healthy risks are vital to the life of the church. Without them, the church atrophies. Its reason for existing collapses into self-care and, after a few years, into self-preservation. Risky and hard things keep gospel blood flowing through the body. Pastor, you cannot afford to coast. You cannot afford autopilot. You owe it to Jesus and to your church to make the most of opportunities in your city—which means that alongside preaching, teaching, praying, and developing leaders, you need to prioritize seeking new avenues for ministry. Be a gospel entrepreneur. Church-planting networks have long understood that entrepreneurial aptitude is essential for planters. But what about established churches—do their pastors need to be entrepreneurial too? What Is a Gospel Entrepreneur? There’s still hesitancy around saying pastors need entrepreneurial aptitude. Maybe it’s because we picture someone who constantly starts new things he can’t sustain—a person with a billion ideas who follows through on none of them. If this is what we mean, then no, we don’t want our pastors to be entrepreneurial. Comfort and complacency are incredibly dangerous. But a gospel entrepreneur is something different. He doesn’t pile up harebrained ideas. He stays awake and sober-minded about the opportunities the Lord is opening in the community. He sees the wooden frames of a new development and prays about how the gospel will reach those families once they move in. He looks at neighborhoods where existing churches can’t possibly reach everyone—and plants a church there. He saves, scrimps, and sacrifices to move a growing church plant into a more strategic location. He keeps his eyes open, his mind sharp, and his hands ready for the moment God opens a door. Biblical Call When this topic comes up, someone usually asks, “Where do you see the need for a pastor to be an entrepreneur in the Bible?” My answer often surprises people: Jesus’s parable of the dishonest manager. In Luke 16:1–9, a rich man discovers his property manager has been wasting his possessions and tells him to settle accounts—he’s about to be fired. The manager realizes losing his job means either digging or begging, so he immediately goes to work cutting deals to gain favor with other wealthy employers. When his employer finds out, he commends the manager for his shrewdness. Ethical or not, it was a genius move. At this point, we should ask, Why is Jesus telling this story? Maybe he’s about to indict people like the manager. But the manager’s dishonesty has nothing to do with Jesus’s point. The twist is that Jesus holds up the dishonest manager as an example of what he wants his disciples to be. “The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness,” Jesus says. “For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light” (Luke 16:

title: The Dangers of Getting Advice from the Internet
summary: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice online and recognize the danger of letting AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ.
summary_zh: Melissa和Courtney讨论了如何在网上寻求建议时培养洞察力，并认识到让人工智能或影响者取代基督身体的明智建议的危险。
title_zh: 从互联网上获取建议的危险
content: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice. They talk about how sometimes we think we need information when what we really need is relationship. They discuss what kind of advice they like to get from the internet or ChatGPT, why they don’t recommend it for wisdom issues such as marriage and parenting, and why we shouldn’t let advice from AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ. Resource Mentioned: Kitchen-Table Counseling Within Your Local Church Related Resources: Let’s Talk: Finding a Mentor and Being a Mentor Want to Grow in Wisdom? You Need Gospel Friends. Why AI Parenting Advice Falls Short Don’t Treat AI as Your Pastor Discussion Questions: 1. When you face a difficult decision or struggle, where do you typically turn for advice? 2. How do you discern whether online advice is helpful or unwise? 3. What makes advice offered within a personal relationship different from advice taken from an online blog or influencer or generated by AI? 4. How might repeated exposure to ideas about marriage, parenting, or relationships on social media influence our thinking without us being aware of it? 5. What do we lose when we turn to online sources for counsel instead of investing in relationships with people who know and love us? 6. Who in your life knows you well enough to speak honestly into your decisions and loves you enough to do so? How can you cultivate those kinds of relationships? 7. How would you like to grow in your ability to offer wise counsel to others?

title: Beware Making Mental Illness an Identity
summary: ‘All in Your Head’ is a concrete and compelling remapping of mental health culture with impressive explanatory power.
summary_zh: “All in Your Head”是对心理健康文化的具体而引人注目的重新映射，具有令人印象深刻的解释力。
title_zh: 小心让精神疾病成为一种身份
content: In the years since he was involuntarily committed to a mental health institution for bipolar disorder, Frederik deBoer has wrestled with both profound gratitude for a system that saved his life and also palpable frustration that his experience of healing has become so rare. All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered is the latest broadside from one of the internet’s most heterodox thinkers and writers. As an “old school” Marxist best known for writing The Cult of Smart , deBoer takes aim at how the cultural drift within his own tribe is responsible for making mental health care so elusive for those who need it most: “The tendency to treat mental illness as an exciting adventure, the endless romanticization of lunacy in popular culture, is one of many aggravations I have nursed for years” (8). The root of his aggravation—the treatment of mental illness and disability as an identity to be celebrated rather than a disability that needs treatment —isn’t all in his head. The use of talk therapy rose 47 percent between 2019 and 2024 . A 2025 LifeStance survey found around 29 percent of U.S. adults have self-diagnosed their mental health condition after consuming online content, rising to 50 percent among Gen Z (versus 9 percent of boomers). Of the people who self-diagnose symptoms, almost a quarter (24 percent) “rarely” or “never” feel the need to take the next step to discuss them with a qualified clinician. DeBoer argues that rather than reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, the inordinate attention given to the mildly and dubiously afflicted is a dangerous distraction crowding out help for the severely ill. Accelerated by social media, this “gentrification of disability” has become a full-blown social contagion, compromising even the experts and institutions responsible for mental health care (153–54). DeBoer is largely right, and the cultural shift he identifies has real-world implications both inside and outside the church. But the same ideological priors that so sharpen deBoer’s critique also suffer from two significant blind spots that, were they addressed, would make All in Your Head the more courageous, more constructive, and, therefore, more widely read manifesto we need. General Bipartisan Ire If you picked up All in Your Head to understand how modern therapy culture spread like wildfire across social media over the last several years, it’s not immediately obvious why deBoer starts his argument with an in-depth analysis of the anti-psychiatry movement’s influence in late 20th century politics and academia. But, if you can forgive me the pun, there’s a method to his madness. After a blistering critique of “rightwing libertarian” policies that neglected mental illness, he cashes in on the subsequent trust he earns with left-leaning readers to launch a series of absolute haymakers toward “a species of thought that sometimes amounts to a kind of leftist pseudo-radicalism or a libertarian fantasy” (198) that drives the “destabilizing . . . move from mental illness as reality to mental illness as symbol” (8). American individualism and anti-institutional bias aren’t new, but the painstakingly specific way deBoer traces their spread through the culture surrounding mental health and therapy is refreshing and instructive. Our “apolitical romanticism of resistance to modern society” fuels two opposite errors: On the right, mental illness is sometimes seen as either imagined or a symptom of weak character. But on the left, the same romanticism often describes mental disability as more en abling than dis abling, as if neurodivergent minorities don’t need society’s help—society needs theirs. Gentrification of Disability DeBoer’s emphatic rejection of this predominantly progressive error— of “making a medical disorder an identity”—is the “overarching principle of [his] book” (165). This is never more clear in what he labels “the gentrification of disability,” where “diagnoses bec
content_zh: 在他非自愿地被送入精神病院治疗两极分化后的几年里,弗雷德里克·德·博尔带着对挽救他生命的系统深表感谢和明显的沮丧,因为他的治愈经验变得如此罕见. 在你的脑海中:作为身份的疾病,作为时尚的创伤,以及希望陷入混乱,是互联网上最异形的思想家和作家之一的最新一面。 作为一位最以写作"聪明的邪教"而出名的"老派"马克思主义者,德博尔以自己的部落内部的文化漂移为目的,让那些最需要的人如此难以接受精神保健:"将精神疾病视为激动人心的冒险的倾向,在流行文化中无休止地浪漫化的放荡,是多年来我所照顾的诸多恶化之一"(8). 他的病情恶化的根源——将精神疾病和残疾视为一种值得庆贺的身份,而不是需要治疗的残疾——并不是他脑子里所有的东西。 2019年至2024年间,谈话疗法的使用率上升了47%. 2025年生活稳定调查发现,约29%的美国成年人在消费了在线内容后自行诊断出自己的心理健康状况,在Gen Z中上升到了50%(相对于9%的繁荣者). 在自我诊断的人群中,近四分之一(24%)的人“勉强”或“从未”感到有必要采取下一步措施,与合格的临床医生讨论这些症状。 DeBoer认为,对受轻度和可疑折磨的人的过度关注,与其减少精神疾病的污名化,不如说是一种危险的分心,挤出对重病患者的帮助。 社交媒体加速了这种 " 残疾意识化 " ,已成为一种全面的社会传染,甚至损害负责精神保健的专家和机构(153-54)。 DeBoer基本上是正确的,他所认定的文化转变在教堂内外都具有现实世界的影响. 但德布尔批评如此尖锐的意识形态前科也遭遇了两个重大盲点,如果这些盲点得到解决,将使你的头脑更加勇敢,更具建设性,因此,我们需要更广泛地阅读宣言。 一般两党爱尔兰人 如果你在脑海中看到现代治疗文化在过去几年里如何像野火一样在社交媒体上传播,那么DeBoer为什么以深入分析20世纪后期反精神病运动在政治和学术界的影响为出发点,这并不明显。 但是,如果你能原谅我的双关语,他疯狂是有办法的。 在对忽视了精神疾病的“右翼自由派”政策猛烈批评后,他依靠后来与左翼读者获得的信任,发动了一系列绝对的干草人,走向“有时相当于一种左翼伪激进主义或自由派幻想的思想”(198年),这种思想驱使“从精神疾病变成现实,转变为精神疾病作为象征”(8)。 美国的个人主义和反机构偏见并非新事物, 但DeBoer通过精神卫生与治疗的文化, 我们“反对现代社会的政治浪漫主义”助长了两个相反的错误: 在右边,精神疾病有时被视为一种想象或一种弱性症状. 但是在左边,同样的浪漫主义常常将精神残疾描述为比分身更困难,仿佛神经分身的少数民族不需要社会的帮助——社会需要他们的帮助。 对DeBoer残疾人的强烈反对,即 " 使医疗障碍成为身份 " 这一主要进步的错误,是 " 书中的首要原则 " (165)。 这在他所称的“残疾的基因化”中再清楚不过了。
author: Brad Edwards

title: How a Former Prisoner in Iran Wants You to Pray for Christians in Chains
summary: Pray not only for what God might do for Christian prisoners in Iran but for what God might do through them, for his glory.
summary_zh: 不仅祈求神可以为伊朗的基督徒囚犯做些什么，而且祈求神可以通过他们为祂的荣耀做些什么。
title_zh: 伊朗前囚犯如何希望你为被锁的基督徒祈祷
content: Not long ago, I had a surreal phone call with two young Christian men serving prison sentences in one of Iran’s hardest prisons. They’re there because they refuse to stop preaching about Jesus. When I asked how I could pray for them, their answer wasn’t what you might expect. “Pray that we would not be released until our job here is finished,” they said. They had led numerous fellow prisoners to faith. Now, their chief concern was to remain inside long enough to disciple them. The call took me straight back to the five years I spent in prison for my faith. Now, these dear brothers (let’s call them Vahid and Reza) were behind bars, and I was outside. As we spoke, I pictured the wards and corridors, imagined the sounds and smells, and remembered how hard it was not to know how many years I would be there. But it was also an encouraging call. Vahid and Reza were in high spirits, talking about Bible passages that were sustaining them and how the Lord was at work. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. Their focus was the same as Paul’s in Colossians 4:3: “Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison.” Paul’s request wasn’t for an open prison door but for an open door for the gospel. Pray for Gospel Fruit Vahid and Reza’s request resonated with me. I remember being unable to pray for my own release. I tried on a few occasions, but I couldn’t open my mouth to ask the Lord to release me. If I’m following Christ, I cannot choose the path. I cannot choose the location. I should follow him wherever he goes. And as I followed him to prison, he brought beautiful fruit. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. I think of one prisoner, a devout Muslim, who was wrongly accused of spying for Iran’s enemies. He was praying he would be released and was frustrated to get no answer. He approached me one day, saying, “Farshid, our God is dead. But I’ve heard yours is alive. Will you pray for me?” Fearing it might be a trap, I took him quietly aside and prayed briefly in the name of Jesus: “Lord, you know this man. Please hear his prayer.” The very next day, the man rushed over excitedly and gave me a huge hug. That morning, he had learned his name had been cleared. He was released two weeks later. Our God is indeed alive. The Lord was also at work softening my parents’ hearts toward Christ during those years. I always say that even if only for the salvation of my parents, my time in prison was worth it. So, when you pray for persecuted believers, pray not only for what God might do for them but—as Vahid and Reza requested—for what God might do through them, for his glory. Pray for gospel fruit. Pray for Comfort and Endurance I don’t want to make prison sound easier than it was. The suffering was real. So pray also for comfort and endurance. They beat me; they broke my toe. But the prolonged separation from my two children was the hardest burden to bear. The day I went to prison, my son was 2 years old and my daughter was 7. Missing their childhoods was an unspeakable loss. Yet I know others who have suffered much more than I did. I think of a brother currently in prison who has been tortured. I think of a sister who was sexually assaulted when she was arrested. Even the apostle Paul was at times “so utterly burdened beyond [his] strength that [he] despaired of life itself.” And his request to the church was simple: “You also must help us by prayer” (2 Cor. 1:8, 11). Brothers and sisters like these need us to pray for them with love. Whatever the situation, we can pray that God would grant the suffering believer comfort, peace, and endurance. The more specific the prayers, the better. While in prison, I received letters from people around the world who were praying for me. One wrote, “I am praying for your sleep. May the Lord give you
content_zh: 不久前,我和两名基督教青年在伊朗最困难的监狱之一服刑。 因为他们拒绝停止宣扬耶稣。 我问自己如何为他们祈祷, 他们说,“祈祷我们在这里的工作结束前不会被释放。” 他们带领许多同狱囚犯信仰。 现在,他们最关心的是 留在里面的时间足够长 让他们入门。 那通电话把我带回我为信仰在监狱里度过的五年。 现在,这些亲爱的兄弟(让我们叫他们Vahid和Reza)在监狱里,我在外面。 就在我们发言的时候,我想象了病房和走廊,想象了声音和气味,并想起了不知道我会在那里呆了多少年是多么困难。 但这也是一个令人鼓舞的呼吁。 瓦希德和礼萨精神高尚,谈论着支撑着他们的圣经段落,以及上帝是如何工作的. 他们并没有看到自己在一个悲惨而黑暗的地方。 他们看到自己在另一个任务领域。 他们的重心与保罗在Colosisans 4:3中的重心相同 : “ 也为我们祈祷,以便上帝为我们打开一个话语之门,宣告基督之谜,我为此而入狱。 ” 保罗的要求并不是打开监狱的门, 祈求福音果实Vahid, 我还记得我无法为自己的自由祈祷 我尝试过几次, 我无法选择道路。 我无法选择位置 我该跟着他 不管他去哪 当我跟着他进监狱时 他带来了美丽的水果 他们并没有看到自己在一个悲惨而黑暗的地方。 他们看到自己在另一个任务领域。 我想到一个囚犯, 一个虔诚的穆斯林, 他祈祷自己会被释放,并因得不到答复而感到沮丧。 有一天,他靠近我说,“法尔希德,我们的神死了。 但我听说你还活着。 你会为我祈祷吗?” 我担心那可能是一个陷阱,悄悄地把他放在一旁,以耶稣的名义简短地祈祷道:"主啊,你认识这个人。 请听他的祈祷。” 第二天,那个男人激动地冲过来,给了我一个巨大的拥抱。 那天早晨,他得知自己的名字已被清除。 他两周后被释放。 我们的神确实还活着。 在那些年中,上帝也在努力使我父母对基督的心软化。 我总是说,即使只是为了拯救我的父母, 我在监狱的时间是值得的。 当你们祈祷受迫害的信士们的时候,你们应当祈祷真主所意欲者,犹如瓦希德和里萨所意欲者那样,祈祷真主所意欲者。 祈取福音果实. 祈祷舒适与耐力, 苦难是真实的。 因此也祈求安慰和耐力. 他们打我,把我的脚趾弄断了 但是,与我的两个孩子长期分离是最难承受的负担。 我入狱那天,我的儿子2岁,女儿7岁。 失去童年是一个难以形容的损失。 然而,我认识其他人,他们遭受的痛苦比我多得多。 我想到目前在监狱里的一个兄弟 曾遭受酷刑 我想到一个妹妹在被捕时曾被性侵犯. 甚至使徒保罗,有时也“承受了超过他力量的沉重负担,以致于他对生命本身绝望”。 他向教堂提出的要求很简单:“你还必须通过祈祷帮助我们”(第1:8、11节)。 这样的兄弟姐妹需要我们用爱为他们祈祷. 无论情况如何,我们可以祈祷上帝会给予受苦受难的信徒以安慰、和平和耐力。 祈祷越具体越好 在狱中,我收到了世界各地为我祈祷的人的来信。 有人写道:“我在为你的睡眠祈祷。 愿主赐予你

title_zh: 圣经重生教义（电子书）
content: Edited by John Hendryx in epub , .mobi & .pdf formats Since faith is infinitely beyond all the power of our unregenerated human nature, it is only God who can give the spiritual ears to hear and eyes to see the beauty of Christ in the gospel. God alone disarms the hostility of the sinner turning his heart of stone to a heart of flesh (2 Cor 4:4-6). It is God, the Holy Spirit, alone who gives illumination and understanding of His word that we might believe; It is God who raises us from the death of sin, who circumcises the heart; unplugs our ears; It is God alone who can give us a new sense, a spiritual capacity to behold the beauty and unsurpassed excellency of Jesus Christ. The apostle John recorded Jesus saying to Nicodemus that we naturally love darkness, hate the light and WILL NOT come into the light (John 3:19, 20). And since our hardened resistance to God is thus seated in our affections, only God, by His grace, can lovingly change, overcome and pacify our rebellious disposition. The natural man, apart from the quickening work of the Holy Spirit, will not come to Christ on his own since he is at enmity with God and cannot understand spiritual things (1 Cor 2:14). Shining a light into a blind man's eyes will not enable him to see, because eyesight first requires a set of healthy eyes.
content_zh: 由John Hendryx在Epub编辑, . 惟有上帝解除了罪人将石心变成肉心的敌意(2 Cor 4:4-6). 只有真主,即圣灵,能照亮和理解我们的信仰; 真主使我们脱离罪恶之死,他割取我们的心;他揭开我们的耳朵; 只有上帝才能给我们一种新的感官,一种精神能力,来见证耶稣基督的美丽和无比杰出。 使徒约翰录制了耶稣对尼克德穆斯说,我们自然地热爱黑暗,憎恨光明并不会进入光明(John 3:19,20). 既然我们对上帝的顽强抵抗 被放在我们的慈爱中 只有上帝能以他的恩惠 慈悲地改变 克服并平息我们的叛逆 自然之人,除了"圣灵"的快活活外,不会独自来到基督,因为他对上帝怀有敌意并无法理解精神事物(1 Cor 2:14). 把一盏光照入一个盲人的眼中不会让他看到,因为视力首先需要一组健康的眼睛.

Our hearts are like fortresses under attack, and we must guard them accordingly. title_zh: 系统神学二
content: by Louis Berkhof In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats You may also download the separate Introductory Volume to Systematic Theology here. Professor Berkhof, who was the President of Calvin Seminary and professor of Systematic Theology at the same in the first half of the twentieth century, has given us an excellent compendium of Reformed theological thought in this hefty volume. The subject is treated in the classical style, moving through the Doctrines of God, Man in Relation to God, the Person and Work of Christ, the Application of the Work of Redemption, the Church and the Means of Grace, and the Last Things. For decades, Louis Berkhof’s Systematic Theology has remained one of the most important and widely-used systematic theologies. It provides the clearest and most succinct articulation of Reformed theology. From its first publication in 1932, Berkhof’s work was revised, reprinted, and translated into Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, and Portuguese, and it had become a standard theological text by 1950. It has gained near-universal use in seminaries and Bible colleges across the world, and is widely cited and used by pastors, theologians, and students of nearly all denominational affiliations.
content_zh: 由路易·伯克霍夫(Louis Berkhof)撰写 在ePub,.mobi和.pdf格式中 您也可以在此下载系统神学的单独入门卷 。 贝尔克霍夫教授曾于20世纪上半叶担任卡尔文神学院院长和系统神学教授,在本书中为我们提供了一份出色的改革神学思想简编. 主题以古典风格来对待,通过"上帝的理论","人与上帝的关系","基督的人与工作","救赎之作的应用","教会与恩赐的手段","最后的事情"等来进行. 数十年来,路易·伯克霍夫的"系统神学"仍然是最重要和被广泛应用的系统神学之一. 它为改革神学提供了最清楚和最简洁的阐述。 从1932年的首次出版起,伯克霍夫的作品被修改,再版,并被翻译成了中文,日文,韩文,西班牙文和葡萄牙文,到1950年已经成为标准的神学文本. 它在世界各地的神学院和圣经学院获得了近乎普遍的使用,并被牧师、神学家和几乎所有教派派别的学生广泛引用和使用。

content: by Thomas Manton in ePub , .mobi & .pdf formats SUCH is the divine matter and admirable order of the Lord’s Prayer, as became the eternal wisdom of God, that composed and dictated it to his disciples. In it are opened the fountains of all our regular petitions, and the arguments contained to encourage our hopes for obtaining them. In our addresses to men, our study is to conciliate their favourable audience; but God is most graciously inclined and ready to grant our requests, therefore we are directed to call upon him by the title of ‘Our Father in heaven,’ to assure us of his love and power, and thereby to excite our reverent attention, to raise our affections, to confirm our confidence in prayer. The supreme end of our desires is the glory of God, in conjunction with our own happiness: this is expressed in the two first petitions, that ‘his name may be hallowed,’ and ‘his kingdom come,’ that we may partake of its felicity. In order to this, our desires are directed for the means that are proper and effectual to accomplish it. And those are of two kinds — the good things that conduct us, and the removal of those evils that obstruct our happiness.
content_zh: 由托马斯·曼顿(Thomas Manton)在ePub所著, . 它打开了我们所有正常请愿书的泉源,并包含了鼓励我们获得这些请愿书的希望的论据。 我们在对人的讲话中,研究是调和他们的好听众;但上帝最慷慨地倾向于并准备同意我们的请求,因此我们奉“我们天上之父”之名号召他,向我们保证他的爱和力量,从而激起我们的敬爱,提高我们的爱心,确认我们对祈祷的信心。 我们欲望的最高目的,是上帝的荣耀,与我们自己的幸福相配合:这在最初的两件请愿书中都有所表述:"他的名字或许是神圣的","他的国来临了",以便我们分享它的荣耀. 为此,我们的愿望是找到适当和有效的手段来实现这一目标。 这些有两种—— 引导我们的好东西, 以及消除那些阻碍我们幸福的邪恶。

In it he defines the concept of dogmatic theology, theology, apologetics, ethics, and science. He also explains the Reformed doctrine of revelation and inspiration. It exxplains what is a theology and how should it be defined? Is theology necessary? What is the task of theology and what are the methods which it should use? What is religion? For those who are considering going to Seminary, to be pastors or simply Christians with ample knowledge of their faith, this is a good book to begin with. This is a very helpful volume in understanding the foundational matters of theology, ranging from the nature of Dogmatics, to the grounds of our knowledge of God, to the doctrines concerning scripture. content: J. C. Ryle "My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all. No one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hand." (John 10:27-29) About the first part of this text, beloved, I spoke to you this morning. I told you then that this passage contains two things—first the character of true Christians, and secondly their privileges—first what they are to their Savior, and secondly what their Savior is to them. Let me, then, remind you what the text says of their character. "My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me." (John 10:27) 1. God's children, His real believing people, are compared to sheep , because they are gentle, quiet, harmless and inoffensive; because they are useful and do good to all around them; because they love to be together, and dislike separation; and lastly because they are very helpless and wandering and liable to stray. 2. Jesus calls them " My sheep ," as if they were His peculiar property. "Mine," He would have us know, by election, "Mine" by purchase, and "Mine" by adoption. 3. Christ's sheep hear His voice, they listen humbly to His teaching, they take His word for their rule and guide. 4. Christ's sheep follow Him, they walk in the narrow path He has marked out, they do not refuse because it is sometimes steep and narrow--but wherever the line of duty lies they go forward without doubting.

Ryle"我的羊听到我的声音,我认识他们,他们跟着我. 我给他们永生 他们永远不会灭亡 没有人会把他们从我手中夺走 我父亲,他给我的,是比所有人更大的。 没有人能把他们从我的父亲手中夺走。” 关于这篇稿子的第一部分,亲爱的,我今天早上跟你谈过了。 我当时告诉你,这段话包含两件事——第一是真正的基督徒的个性,第二是他们的特权——第一是他们的救世主,第二是他们的救世主。 那么,让我提醒你, 文字上说他们的性格。 我的羊听见我的声音,就认识他们,他们顺从我。 真主的儿子,他的忠实的信徒,被比喻为羊,因为他们是温和的,安静的,无害的,是无罪的;因为他们是有用的,是对他们周围的人都有益的;因为他们爱在一起,不喜欢分离;最后,因为他们非常无助,而且游荡而容易迷失。 2. 耶稣称他们为"我的羊",好像他们是他的特有财产. "我",他会让我们知道,通过选举,"我"通过购买,"我"通过收养。 3. 基督的羊听到 他的声音,他们恭敬地听从他的教诲,他们以他的话为他们的统治和向导. 4. 基督的羊跟随他, 他们走在狭窄的道路 他已指出,他们不会拒绝,因为有时是陡峭和狭窄的,但无论在哪里,他们都毫不怀疑地前进。

title_zh: 关于宗教体验的思考（电子书）
content: by Archibald Alexander In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats On the basis of fifty years as a pastor, preacher and professor at Princeton Theological Seminary, Archibald Alexander (1772-1851) deals with the subjective work of the Holy Spirit in the heart in all its phases, from the new birth until final preparation for heaven. There are two kinds of religious knowledge which, though intimately connected as cause and effect, may nevertheless be distinguished. These are the knowledge of the truth as it is revealed in the Holy Scriptures; and the impression which that truth makes on the human mind when rightly apprehended. The first may be compared to the inscription or image on a seal, the other to the impression made by the seal on the wax. When that impression is clearly and distinctly made, we can understand, by contemplating it, the true inscription on the seal more satisfactorily, than by a direct view of the seal itself. Thus it is found that nothing tends more to confirm and elucidate the truths contained in the Word, than an inward experience of their efficacy on the heart. It cannot, therefore, be uninteresting to the Christian to have these effects, as they consist in the various views and affections of the mind, traced out and exhibited in their connection with the truth, and in their relation to each other.
content_zh: 由Archibald Alexander In ePub , .mobi 和.pdf格式编辑 。 在担任普林斯顿神学院牧师,传道人和教授50年的基础上,阿奇博尔德·亚历山大(1772年-1851年)处理从新出世到最后准备上天等各个阶段的心灵圣灵的主观工作. 宗教知识有两种,虽然作为因果关系有着密切的联系,但仍可加以区分。 这些是《圣经》中所揭示的真理的知识;以及真理在人心上所留下的正确捕捉的印象。 第一种可以和封印上所刻的铭文或图像相提并论,另一种可以和蜡上所刻的封印的印象相提并论. 当这种印象清楚而明显地形成时,我们可以通过考虑它来理解印章上的真正铭文,比直接看到印章本身更令人满意。 因此,人们发现,最能证实和阐明《言语》中包含的真理的莫过于内在的内心体验。 因此,基督教徒对这些影响不能不感兴趣,因为这些影响包含在思想的各种观点和感情中,在他们与真理的关系上,以及在他们与彼此的关系上,被追溯和表现出来。

content: BY JOHN OWEN IN .EPUB , .MOBI & .PDF FORMATS Formatted, lightly modernized and spelling corrections by Denise Kristiansson To design of the ensuing Discourse is to declare some part of that glory of our Lord Jesus Christ which is revealed in the Scripture, and proposed as the principal object of our faith, love, delight, and admiration. But, alas! after our utmost and most diligent inquiries, we must say, How little a portion is it of him that we can understand! His glory is incomprehensible, and his praises are unutterable. Some things an illuminated mind may conceive of it; but what we can express in comparison of what it is in itself, is even less than nothing. But as for those who have forsaken the only true guide herein, endeavouring to be wise above what is written, and to raise their contemplations by fancy and imagination above Scripture revelation (as many have done), they have darkened counsel without knowledge, uttering things which they understand not, which have no substance or spiritual food of faith in them.

title_zh: 时髦人士和其他世俗主义者的护教学
content: "Although They Knew God ... They Suppressed the Truth..." The opportunities are wide open for Christians to speak with secular people these days, especially if you live in a metropolitan area. The average hipster you may meet in the medium to big sized city is a secularist who may listen to NPR, has a liberal, ecological, and/or anti-capitalist political ideology ... wears vintage clothing from a thrift store and consumes ethically. He or she often either rides a bike, uses public transportation or even may be driving a hybrid or bio-diesel vehicle. This person is deeply concerned with the ethical treatment of animals, is strongly against slavery, torture, racism and political oppression against women. In other words, he takes morality very seriously. Another characteristic of this individual is that he/she thinks Christianity is irrelevant at best. Since we deeply care about the eternal destinies of such individuals how should we go about reaching such a person with the gospel? Where would you start? Once of the more effective ways, I have found, is to remember that that your secular friend already knows God exists. He/she knows God exists and lives as if He does. In Romans chapter 1 Paul clearly teaches this about all people when he says, "For although they knew God" (verse 21) "...by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (verse 18). But how can we demonstrate to your friends that they already believe in God, when intellectually they deny His existence? While there are many ways this could be done, I would like to suggest one way that I have found to be quite persuasive: The knowledge of God through their own morality.
content_zh: "虽然他们认识上帝... 这些天基督徒与世俗人士交谈的机会是广阔的,特别是如果你生活在一个都市地区. 在中等至大城市中,你可能遇到的平凡的嬉皮士是一个世俗主义者,他可能听从NPR,具有自由主义,生态主义和/或反资本主义的政治意识形态.穿着节俭店出产的古装并合乎道德地消费. 他或她往往要么骑自行车,使用公共交通,要么甚至可能驾驶混合或生物柴油车辆. 此人对动物的道德待遇深感关切,强烈反对奴役、酷刑、种族主义和对妇女的政治压迫。 换句话说,他非常重视道德。 这个人的另一个特征是,heshe认为基督教最多是无关紧要的. 既然我们深深地关心这些人的永恒命运,那么我们如何用福音去帮助这样一个人呢? 你从哪里开始? 我发现,最有效的方法之一 就是记住,你的世俗朋友已经知道上帝的存在。 他/她知道上帝的存在 并活得像他一样 在罗马人第一章中,保罗明确教导了这一点,他说:"虽然他们认识上帝"(第21节)"......以不义压制真理"(第18节). 但我们怎能向你的朋友证明,他们已经信仰了真主,而他们在理智上否认他的存在呢? 虽然有许多方法可以做到这一点,但我想建议一种方法,我认为它很有说服力: 以自德而知神.

title: Prison Didn’t Mean Paul Was Wrong
summary: Steven Morales explains why following Jesus is worth every sacrifice, even when faithfulness leads to suffering and imprisonment.
summary_zh: 史蒂文·莫拉莱斯（ Steven Morales ）解释了为什么即使忠诚导致痛苦和监禁，跟随耶稣也是值得的。
title_zh: 监狱并不意味着保罗错了
content: “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.” (Eph. 4:1) Those are weighty words. And they’re weighty not because Paul is writing from a quiet study or a place of comfort, but because he is writing them from a prison cell. Paul isn’t sending this letter from a position of safety or success as the world defines it. He’s writing as a man in chains—arrested for preaching the gospel and planting churches. To his critics, he was a troublemaker. A dangerous agitator. To God, he was a faithful servant . That matters. Paul is suffering for the very message he’s urging the church in Ephesus to remember and live out. His words carry weight because his life backs them up. He’s not asking them to do anything he himself isn’t already doing—at great personal cost. And here’s the remarkable thing about Paul: there is no scenario in which he loses. Let him go free, and he’ll travel to the ends of the earth preaching Christ and starting churches. Lock him up, and he’ll become “a prisoner for the Lord,” turning his suffering into a living testimony of the worth of the gospel. Execute him? Fine. As he says elsewhere, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21, ESV). There is no situation where Paul says, “The gospel isn’t enough anymore.” There is no moment where he concludes, “This just isn’t worth it.” Instead, Paul’s entire life—especially his suffering—testifies to this truth: no matter your circumstances, trusting in the gospel is never wasted. Paul wasn’t in prison because his ministry failed. He was in prison because he believed the message was worth suffering for. And that’s an important distinction. If a message isn’t worth suffering for, it’s probably not worth believing in. Christianity doesn’t promise a life without pain. What it promises is something better: a suffering that is not meaningless. A hope that suffering does not get the final word. That’s why Paul can say this in 2 Corinthians: “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” (2 Co. 4:17–18) The gospel gives us a framework for enduring temporary suffering because it anchors us in permanent promises. We can endure hardship now because we know it won’t last forever. Our pain has an expiration date . Why? Because Jesus has already suffered fully in our place. He took sin, death, and judgment upon himself—and walked out of the grave victorious. Because of him, not even death has the final say over us. So when Paul urges believers to “walk in a manner worthy of the calling,” he’s not laying a burden on their shoulders. He’s inviting them into a life shaped by hope—a life that knows that whatever it costs to follow Jesus, it will never be in vain. title: Five Ways to Pray for Persecuted Christians
summary: Jamie Dean offers a prayer guide for persecuted Christians in Iran, China, North Korea, and other hard to reach nations.
summary_zh: 杰米·迪恩（ Jamie Dean ）为伊朗、中国、朝鲜和其他难以抵达的国家的受迫害基督徒提供了祈祷指南。
title_zh: 为受迫害的基督徒祈祷的五种方式
content: Sunday, Nov. 1, marks the annual International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church. It’s a day for believers across the globe to unite in concentrated prayer for Christians suffering for the gospel. Here are a few biblically-based ways to pray for the persecuted, along with a guide to a few specific nations to remember. 1. PRAY FOR THOSE IN PRISON “Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them.” Hebrews 13:3 Iran : In 2025, Christians were sentenced to a combined total of more than 280 years in prison . Pray for those still in jail, and for families enduring separation. China : The Chinese government has continued its crackdown on believers, including several still in prison after a raid on Zion Church last year . Pray for gospel hope and perseverance. Eritrea : As many as 350 believers remained in jails in 2025, including some who have been imprisoned for decades . Pray for endurance and deliverance. 2. PRAY FOR BOLDNESS “And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness.” Acts 4: 29 Syria, Pakistan , Libya , Sudan : Danger and threats are a common experience for believers in these nations. Pray for the Lord to protect churches and give them boldness to proclaim Christ, even when it’s difficult. 3. PRAY THAT PEOPLE WILL COME TO KNOW JESUS “I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel.” Philippians 1:12 Afghanistan : In a country where it’s more dangerous than ever to follow Jesus, Afghans are still coming to know him. Pray believers will continue to be a witness, and that unbelievers will find true life in Christ. 4. PRAY FOR GOD’S BLESSING TO THOSE SUFFERING “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven…Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.” Matthews 5:10,12 North Korea, Somalia, Yemen: These are among the most difficult places in the world to follow Christ. Pray for the Lord to bless these believers facing severe persecution, and to strengthen them with the hope of heaven. 5. PRAY FOR THE PERSECUTORS “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” Matthew 5:44 Nigeria: Christians in northern Nigeria have endured kidnappings and violence for years. Pray the Lord will stop their attackers, and use the believers’ witness to draw persecutors to himself. For more ways to pray for the persecuted church, grab a copy of Pray the World , a 31-day devotional for hard to reach nations.

title: Standing with Brothers and Sisters We Cannot See
summary: David Platt shares a powerful story of forgiveness and challenges Christians to support persecuted believers through prayer.
summary_zh: 大卫·普拉特（ David Platt ）分享了一个关于宽恕的强大故事，并挑战基督徒通过祈祷来支持受迫害的信徒。
title_zh: 与我们看不到的兄弟姐妹站在一起
content: I remember the first time I stood at the demilitarized zone, or the DMZ, on the border between North and South Korea. I looked across this dividing line, knowing that on the other side I (and we) have brothers and sisters who are suffering and dying for following Jesus and making him known. I think about Soon Yangown, a pastor in a leper colony during the Japanese occupation of the Korean peninsula many years ago. He refused to worship the shrines that had been set up for the Korean people to worship, so he was arrested and imprisoned. When the Japanese occupation ended, he was released. Years later, his two oldest sons, Tongin and Tongsin, were in middle school when a mob representing the communist party came to their campus. The boys were known to be strong Christians, so the mob brought them out of the school and began to beat them. Eventually, a leader of the mob named Ahn shot and killed both the boys. By the time Pastor Soon heard of his sons’ death, the revolt had been quieted, and his sons’ killer had been apprehended. Upon hearing this news, Pastor Soon immediately sent a messenger to the court to plead for them to spare Ahn. The judge agreed to do so, and Pastor Soon then offered to adopt Ahn as his own son. Years later, communists invaded the leper colony where Pastor Soon was pastoring. He refused to flee and chose to stay with the church. He was arrested, imprisoned, tied up with 75 other followers of Jesus, and executed. I wish these stories were only from the past. Unfortunately, however, suffering, persecution, and martyrdom are present-day realities for our brothers and sisters in North Korea. So what can we do for them? For starters, we can remember them and learn about what they are experiencing. In the words of Hebrews 13:3: “Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.” We can take time to listen to and learn the story of our family in North Korea as if we were with them in North Korea. (Radical’s documentary Hard to Reach: North Korea is a good place to start.) As you remember our brothers and sisters in North Korea and other hard lands , I invite you to pray for them. Let your prayers be guided by Paul’s exhortation in Ephesians 6:18–20 for the church to pray for him while he was in prison: “To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.” Finally, let’s join them. They’re giving their lives to share the gospel with people around them. If you’re reading this, the likelihood is that your life is not at stake in the same way as theirs. But you can still give your life to what they’re giving their lives to: speaking the gospel and sharing God’s love in Jesus with the people you and I interact with today. Let’s lock arms with our brothers and sisters in North Korea , following Jesus and making him known no matter what it costs, because we know that he is our reward.
